docs.title: Dokicraft
docs.text:
A high-fidelity voxel survival game engine built from scratch in C++ — Minecraft-like gameplay with smaller voxels, modern Vulkan rendering, advanced lighting, and streamed worlds.

Docs site: https://dougfessler.com/projects/dokicraft/ (tutorial, research, plan, and test docs, rebuilt automatically on every push to main).

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Renders a voxel scene. The from-scratch Vulkan engine boots a window, selects the discrete GPU, and draws a lit heightmapped voxel terrain via dynamic rendering.

Architecture is settled (see research.md); roadmap and current state live in plan.md. Next: chunked streaming worlds and binary greedy meshing.

New to the codebase? Start with the tutorial: tutorial.md. It's a full walkthrough of how the engine works and how to extend it, written for developers coming from Unreal Engine.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Visual Studio 2022+ (2026 recommended) with the C++ workload, CMake 3.28+, Ninja, Git.

git clone https://github.com/defessler/Dokicraft.git
cd Dokicraft
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg.git extern/vcpkg
extern\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat -disableMetrics

Then, from a Developer Command Prompt / PowerShell for VS (so cl and the Windows SDK are on PATH):

cmake --preset windows-release
cmake --build --preset windows-release

Or, from any shell, let the helper locate and enter the VS environment for you:

pwsh -File Tools/Build.ps1                 # release
pwsh -File Tools/Build.ps1 -Preset windows-debug

The first configure builds all dependencies from source via vcpkg and takes a while; subsequent builds are incremental. The compiled game lands at build/<preset>/bin/dokicraft.exe.

The Vulkan SDK is not required — Vulkan headers, the volk loader, and the shaderc shader compiler all come from vcpkg; only a Vulkan-capable GPU driver is needed at runtime.

docs.title: Dokicraft — Research Deep Dives
docs.text:
This page is meant as a quick reference on the second verified research pass and what it settled. The first report ended with four open questions and a list of coverage gaps. This pass went after them directly: 6 search angles, 30 sources fetched, 147 claims extracted, 25 adversarially verified by 3-vote panels, 24 confirmed and 1 refuted, synthesized to the 12 findings below (run wf_ff842636-3e8, 113 agents, 2026-07-12). Anything that didn't survive verification is listed as a gap rather than asserted.

One reading rule up front: every measured benchmark below predates Blackwell (the test hardware spans an integrated GPU, Turing, and Ampere), so treat absolute numbers as illustrative and carry only the relative rankings and architectural conclusions to our RTX 5090 target.

docs.title: 1. Hardware Ray Tracing For Voxels: The Direction Is Settled
docs.text:
The first report couldn't say whether hardware RT beats software voxel traversal. It now looks settled in hardware RT's favor, on three independent lines of evidence:

  • The strongest measurement - Peer-reviewed JCGT paper (Hansson-Söderlund, Evans, and Akenine-Möller of NVIDIA, 2022): on an RTX 3090, path tracing up to three bounces, a DXR BVH built over all non-empty voxels with a custom intersection shader beat pure shader-based traversal by roughly 3 to 5x on complex scenes. Their "Ladies" scene ran 16.1 ms versus 79.7 ms for grid sphere tracing and 54.8 ms for shader-traversed SVO ("Heads" is closer to 2.4 to 2.9x). A 2023 follow-up with tighter AABBs gained a further 20 to 31%. Caveat: their scenes are trilinearly interpolated SDF grids, not opaque cube voxels, so our intersection shaders would differ. HIGH confidence, 3-0.
  • The architecture proof - A peer-reviewed ISVC 2024 paper ran custom voxel traversal inside the hardware RT pipeline (procedural AABB path, custom intersection and closest-hit shaders, RTX 2060 Super via Vulkan) and found hybrid hierarchical formats reach a new Pareto frontier of speed versus storage, up to 2.1x. The takeaway for us isn't the specific formats. It's the existence proof that software voxel logic inside hardware intersection shaders is a viable production architecture. HIGH confidence, 3-0.
  • The compute-side corroboration - VoxelRT's benchmarks (integrated GPU, so rankings only): a plain binary BVH with DDA brick leaves is already competitive with specialized voxel structures on primary rays (175.0 Mrays/s on Sponza 2k versus Tree64's 182.6), and it's the one structure that gains RT-core acceleration on real hardware, which the iGPU test couldn't even exercise. It does fall behind on incoherent diffuse rays (102 versus ~125 Mrays/s). MEDIUM confidence, 3-0.

What did not survive: the claim that greedy meshing only buys ~15% for ray traversal was refuted 0-3, so the "hardware BVH over greedy-meshed triangle quads versus per-voxel AABBs" question has no verified answer at all. That one needs an in-engine microbenchmark when far-field work starts. It's cheap to build both paths on our stack since bufferDeviceAddress and the RT extensions are one device-feature request away.

docs.title: 2. Global Illumination: Still Mostly Open, Honestly
docs.text:
This is the section where verification did its job by killing false confidence. Nothing comparative survived on flood-fill lighting, voxel cone tracing, or ReSTIR-plus-denoiser pipelines. The only GI datapoint that survived is an existence proof:

  • Compute-only DDGI works in voxel worlds - A Vulkan DDGI implementation for Minecraft-style scenes ran entirely on a compute-shader path tracer because the team's GPUs lacked the RT extension: 250 FPS on a Cornell-box scene with three lights, dropping to 29 FPS in a larger cave scene with four lights. It proves DDGI doesn't require hardware RT, and it warns that probe and light count scaling bites hard. LOW confidence on the numbers (a ~2020 student project, GPU model unstated, honest about its own unflattering results). 3-0.

Our plan doesn't change: sun plus ambient occlusion first, DDGI phase 2 (Dwyer's devlog from the first pass remains the strongest practitioner evidence). The flood-fill versus DDGI versus ReSTIR comparison stays on the open-questions list, and given finding 1, an RT-backed probe tracer on the 5090 is now the likelier phase-2 shape than a compute one.

docs.title: 3. LOD And Streaming: Aokana Is The Template
docs.text:
The first pass established Aokana (peer-reviewed, I3D 2025) renders ten-billion-voxel scenes. This pass extracted its architecture in enough detail to use:

  • World structure - The map divides into axis-aligned cubic regions, each backed by a 256^3-voxel chunk.
  • LOD scheme - A LOD n chunk keeps 256^3 resolution but covers 8x the volume of LOD n-1, built by aggregating each 2x2x2 group of child voxels into one (kept when at least 2 of 8 children are non-empty, color averaged) across 2x2x2 child-chunk groups.
  • Streaming - Only ~5% of scene data stays resident in VRAM during navigation. At 64K resolution, San Miguel needs 424 MB of VRAM against 23.2 GB on disk, about 2%.
  • Measured cost - ~6 ms average frames at 64K resolution on an RTX 3060 Ti, 2 to 4x faster than HashDAG on average above 32K (peaks of 4.8x speed and ~8 to 9x memory are peaks, not averages). HIGH confidence, 3-0, with the caveat that the numbers are the authors' own and the HashDAG baseline prioritizes editability over throughput.

The honest limit: Aokana ray traces SVDAGs directly, so it never faces the problem our near field has. Nothing survived on LOD seam and crack handling for meshed chunk geometry, and nothing survived on mesh shaders for voxel quads. Both stay open. For the far field, though, region grouping plus 8-to-1 aggregation is now our working template rather than a research pointer.

docs.title: 4. Persistence: Pick Your Compression Granularity Deliberately
docs.text:
New territory this pass, and it produced the clearest design guidance of the six topics:

  • Anvil's two waste sources - Minecraft's region format pads every chunk to 4096-byte sector boundaries and compresses each chunk independently with zlib, which caps the compression context. Both are confirmed against the format spec.
  • Whole-region compression halves disk - The Linear format compresses an entire 32x32-chunk region as a single zstd stream and saves roughly 50% on typical overworld data. The figure is corroborated twice over: the README's own worked example (227 GB to 120 GB, 47.3%) and an independent measurement on a different world (48.3%). The ~95% figure for The End is self-reported only. zstd itself is ~5x faster than zlib, consistent with Meta's published benchmarks. MEDIUM confidence, 3-0.
  • The tradeoff is real and verified in code - One stream per region means decompressing the whole region to read any chunk. There's no per-chunk seek table, and the verifier confirmed the mechanism in the reference implementation rather than trusting the README. Successor formats (Linear v2 buckets, SectorTool, SHARD) exist specifically to fix this. MEDIUM confidence, 3-0.

Design implication for Dokicraft, recorded for the persistence phase: compression granularity (per chunk, per region, or bucketed) is an explicit tradeoff between ratio and random-access streaming, zstd is the default codec, and the version tag plus migration path from our J5 convention applies to whatever container we pick.

docs.title: 5. Worldgen: FastNoise2 Confirmed, The Rest Still Open
docs.text:
• The architecture holds up - FastNoise2 compiles its generators for Scalar, SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX512, NEON, and WASM SIMD and picks the fastest supported level at runtime. Its node graph (fractals, domain warps, blends composing as nodes) executes fused inside the SIMD pipeline with intermediates staying in registers, which is precisely what makes deep layered noise stacks cheap. Graphs can be authored visually in the bundled Node Editor and serialized to compact strings the runtime loads with NewFromEncodedNodeTree, so designers can iterate on terrain without an engine recompile. HIGH confidence, 3-0, mechanisms verified in source.
  • The speed claim is directional but large - The author's benchmarks show ~5 to 7x over scalar FastNoise Lite (268 versus 37 million points/sec for 3D simplex on AVX2). Author-reported, on a 2020-era CPU, and the simplex row compares slightly different algorithm variants, so carry the direction rather than the ratio. MEDIUM confidence, 3-0.
  • Two practical notes from verification - The project recommends ClangCL over MSVC on Windows for the SIMD paths, worth knowing for our toolchain. Cross-version compatibility of encoded node-tree strings isn't documented as guaranteed, so treat them like any other versioned asset.

Biome blending, cave generation (3D noise versus worms), and structure placement produced no surviving claims. Those get decided by prototyping at the worldgen phase, not by citation.

docs.title: 6. Physics Under Edits: The Rebuild Pattern Is Canonical
docs.text:
The first pass covered static terrain. This pass filled in what happens when the world changes, and the guidance converges from three primary sources (the Jolt author's discussions, Jolt's official docs, and a production Godot fix):

  • The canonical shape strategy - A regular grid of tiles, one StaticCompoundShape per tile, rebuilding only the affected tile's compound on change. The author calls these "fairly cheap to create at run-time" and suggests keeping tiles small, 16^3, warning that 16x256x16 "may already be too much". HIGH confidence, 3-0.
  • The burst-edit refinement - StaticCompoundShape costs more to create than MutableCompoundShape because it builds internal spatial partitioning at creation, trading construction time for query speed. Godot's Jolt module used to rebuild the static compound from scratch on every edit; the merged Godot 4.4 fix builds the cheaper mutable variant while edits are in flight and defers the upgrade to static until the next physics step. That's a directly reusable pattern for edit-heavy voxel play (digging, building). Sub-shapes are cached between rebuilds, so the rebuild cost is the compound container, not every block. HIGH confidence, 3-0.
  • The hard no - MeshShape is not runtime-editable and never will be: "The MeshShape really wasn't made to be updated at run time", creation "was always meant to be an offline process". Runtime updates were deliberately added to HeightFieldShape and MutableCompoundShape through v5.6.0 and never to MeshShape. Per-tile MeshShape rebuilds remain acceptable. HIGH confidence, 3-0.

The gap: no measured broadphase-churn or debris-body numbers survived for Teardown-scale destruction rates. When destruction lands, we profile Jolt's own tiled pattern under a synthetic edit storm rather than trusting anyone's forum estimate.

docs.title: What This Changes In The Plan
docs.text:
• Far field and RT - Hardware BVH over per-voxel AABBs with custom intersection shaders is promoted from open question to leading candidate. An in-engine microbenchmark (triangle BVH over greedy quads versus AABB plus intersection shader) gets scheduled when far-field work starts.
  • Streaming - Aokana's region grouping and 8-to-1 LOD aggregation become the far-field template. Meshed-LOD seam handling still needs its own answer.
  • Persistence - zstd, an explicit granularity decision, and versioned containers go into the §5 persistence design.
  • Worldgen - FastNoise2 confirmed. Encoded node trees become the designer-facing terrain format. Evaluate ClangCL for the worldgen-heavy targets.
  • Physics - The tile-plus-StaticCompound rebuild pattern with the mutable-during-bursts refinement is the adopted integration design.
  • GI - Unchanged (sun plus AO, then DDGI), with the phase-2 tracer now likelier to ride hardware RT.

docs.title: Refuted This Pass
docs.text: • ~~"Greedy meshing yields only about a 15% traversal improvement (up to 20x in special cases)"~~ - killed 0-3. Don't cite it, here or elsewhere.

docs.title: Remaining Open Questions
docs.text:
1. On Blackwell hardware, does a triangle BVH over greedy-meshed quads beat an AABB BVH with custom intersection shaders for opaque cube voxels? Needs our own microbenchmark.
  2. Flood-fill versus voxel cone tracing versus DDGI versus ReSTIR-plus-denoiser in a small-voxel survival world: no comparative measurements exist anywhere we could verify.
  3. LOD seam/crack handling for meshed voxel chunks, and whether mesh shaders help voxel quad geometry at all.
  4. Broadphase churn and debris management costs in Jolt at destruction scale: answered only by profiling.

docs.title: Dokicraft — high-fidelity voxel survival game engine in C++
Context
docs.text:
Dokicraft is a from-scratch C++ game engine and survival game: Minecraft-like gameplay but at a higher fidelity level — smaller voxels, modern shaders and lighting, streamed worlds. Solo/small-team project targeting Windows x64 and high-end GPUs (primary dev/target machine has an RTX 5090). The user's stated tech preferences, honored unless research shows a clear winner elsewhere: open-source rendering API (Vulkan), open-source UI framework (Dear ImGui; web-tech HTML/CSS style highly preferred but only if high performance), and "Box3D" physics (no such library exists — read as "a 3D physics engine"; research evaluates Jolt / Bullet / PhysX).

docs.title: Dokicraft — Architecture Research Report

Method: 5 search angles → 24 sources fetched → 119 claims extracted → top 25 adversarially verified (3-vote panels) → 24 confirmed, 1 refuted → synthesized to the 11 findings below. docs.title: 1. Binary greedy meshing is the CPU meshing best practice — HIGH (3-0)
docs.text: Meshes a 64³-padded chunk in 50–200 µs single-threaded (avg 74 µs, Ryzen 3800X) by culling and merging 64 faces at a time with bitwise ops on binary occupancy masks. Output is 8 bytes/quad (6-bit x/y/z/width/height, vertex pulling), drawn in a single glMultiDrawElementsIndirect call. Verified in code, not just README; independently reimplemented (omar-owis/VoxelEngine, multiple Rust ports — Inspirateur's is ~30× faster than block-mesh-rs). Caveats: 64³ cap includes neighbor padding (62³ meshable); merging does per-quad voxel-type lookups; benchmark excludes block-type data prep. Sources: cgerikj/binary-greedy-meshing, omar-owis/VoxelEngine, grobert.eu/voxel-techniques

docs.title: 2. Acceleration structures for ray-traced voxels: wide trees > SVOs; brickmaps diverge — HIGH (3-0)
docs.text: Wide 4³-branching trees (Tree64): ~209 Mrays/s primary vs ESVO's 57–137 in VoxelRT's benchmarks, best incoherent-ray ratio (~0.89×). Brickmap multi-level DDA is competitive on coherent primary rays (147.7 Mrays/s) but collapses on incoherent secondary rays (0.44×; plain DDA 0.10×) from SIMD divergence. Triangle-style BVH is among the fastest (~216 Mrays/s) and is the hardware-accelerated path. Caveat: all measured on an iGPU — author estimates 5–10× on discrete; rankings may shift on RTX hardware. Source: dubiousconst282/VoxelRT

docs.title: 3. GPU-driven rendering + tiny chunks (Ascendant pattern) — HIGH (3-0)
docs.text: With 8×8×8 chunks, ~400,000 chunks can be in view — CPU culling is a non-starter; a compute shader frustum/occlusion-culls and writes indirect draw commands + count. Far field abandons meshing for one quad per voxel with ray/box intersection in the pixel shader (Majercik et al., JCGT 2018; costs MSAA). This near-mesh/far-raycast hybrid with GPU submission is the concrete pattern for small-voxel worlds at scale. Source: vkguide.dev Ascendant geometry

docs.title: 4. Vulkan is the evidence-backed API choice — HIGH (3-0)
docs.text: Ascendant (most complete documented small-voxel engine) is Vulkan; Dwyer implemented a new Vulkan renderer for performance after building on wgpu/WebGPU. A fully GPU-driven pipeline is achievable on OpenGL 4.6 AZDO (verified in code) — so the API choice is about hardware RT, mesh shaders, and ecosystem, not a capability wall. No verified Vulkan-vs-DX12 head-to-head survived. Sources: vkguide Ascendant, Dwyer devlog #23, omar-owis/VoxelEngine

docs.title: 5. Streaming/LOD: many shallow per-chunk SVDAGs, not one deep one — HIGH (3-0)
docs.text: Aokana (peer-reviewed, i3D 2025): one SVDAG per 256³ chunk; CPU octree filters chunks for async load/unload; only ~5% of scene data resident in VRAM; per-chunk distance LOD. Renders tens of billions of voxels at ~6 ms average on an RTX 3060 Ti (2–4× faster than HashDAG baseline). Caveats: static scenes, opaque voxels, simple shading, screen res unstated — proves primary visibility at scale, not destructibility or GI. Source: Aokana, arXiv 2505.02017

docs.title: 6. GI: probe-based DDGI is the demonstrated practical choice — MEDIUM (3-0, single source)
docs.text: Dwyer replaced path tracing with DDGI ("less noisy, more efficient"); supports dark caves, bright exteriors, matte/shiny/emissive materials. Pattern: once-per-model probe bake (16-voxel grid cells, BFS probe placement toward largest empty subnode, 4 probe LODs) + per-frame compute culling (active-probe worklist) + fixed total ray budget → stable frame cost. Caveat: N=1 first-person devlog; no surviving comparison vs flood-fill, VCT, or HW-RT path tracing. Source: Dwyer Voxel Devlog #23

docs.title: 7. Physics: Jolt with author-prescribed voxel integration — HIGH (3-0)
docs.text: jrouwe's own guidance: one Body + StaticCompoundShape per chunk (keep chunks small — 16³; 16×256×16 "may already be too much"), reuse shared BoxShapes per block size; "100K static bodies should not be an issue, so even if you have 5000 chunks loaded it should be fine." Caveats: edits rebuild the chunk's compound shape and wake sleeping bodies; batch-add + OptimizeBroadPhase; dynamic-destruction performance is an open question. Source: JoltPhysics discussion #446

docs.title: 8. UI: Ultralight legitimate but encumbered; RmlUi is the FOSS path — MEDIUM
docs.text: Ultralight is GPU-accelerated HTML/CSS/JS purpose-built for game embedding (GPUDriver API). But its "~10× lower memory than Chromium" marketing claim was refuted 0-3 in verification; core is proprietary (free only < $100K/yr revenue), not thread-safe, no WebGL/video. RmlUi: fully FOSS, retained-mode, bring-your-own-renderer, no built-in JS. Dear ImGui remains the zero-risk debug/tooling default. Sources: ultralig.ht, RmlUi discussion #331

docs.title: 9. ECS: EnTT vs flecs is not perf-decisive — MEDIUM (single microbenchmark)
docs.text: abeimler/ecs_benchmark complex-update (~2M entities, Linux/GCC 14.2): flecs 4.0.1 42 ms vs EnTT 3.13.2 views 85 ms (groups 87, runtime-views 184, stable 51; mustache fastest at 33). Iteration/storage choices matter as much as library. Choose on ergonomics. Caveats: single benchmark, not on Windows/MSVC, both libs have newer releases. Source: abeimler/ecs_benchmark

docs.title: 10. Traversal fundamentals: DDA over fixed-step for small voxels — MEDIUM (one 2-1 vote)
docs.text: Amanatides & Woo DDA needed ~10.5M ray iterations vs 33.8M–130.4M for fixed-step marching (steps 0.2→0.05) in Grobert's thesis testbed — the textbook result; constants are scene-dependent. Sources: grobert.eu/voxel-techniques, Notiooo/Voxel-Techniques

  • cgerikj/binary-greedy-meshing — the meshing reference.
  • vkguide Ascendant series — production Vulkan small-voxel engine, our closest blueprint.
  • omar-owis/VoxelEngine — GPU-driven OpenGL 4.6.
  • Aokana paper — SVDAG streaming at scale.
  • Grobert thesis + testbed — technique survey.
  • Douglas Dwyer devlogs — DDGI, Vulkan migration.

Q1 (hardware RT) now has a settled direction, Q2 (Jolt under edits) has a canonical integration pattern, and streaming, persistence, and worldgen gained verified findings. docs.title: Cross-check: Hazel Engine (StudioCherno/Hazel, release 2024.1)
docs.text:
Added at user request as a real-world reference stack, with the explicit instruction to validate, not blindly adopt. Hazel is TheCherno's general-purpose 2D/3D engine (Apache-2.0; premake build; an editor Hazelnut, a runtime, and C# scripting via Coral). Facts below are read directly from its Dependencies.lua and .gitmodules at commit d16adf5, not from memory.

The load-bearing caveat: Hazel is a traditional PBR triangle-mesh / scene-graph renderer, not a voxel engine. Its rendering paradigm (mesh rasterization, material system, Assimp-imported models) does not transfer to Dokicraft's voxel-specific pipeline (binary greedy meshing, GPU-driven culling, SVDAG/raycast far-field, DDGI) — findings §1–§6 above still govern rendering. What Hazel usefully validates is the engine-infrastructure layer around the renderer.

docs.title: Independently corroborates our settled stack (same choice, arrived at separately)
docs.text: Our pick Hazel uses Note Vulkan Vulkan (vulkan-1, requires VULKAN_SDK) Confirms Vulkan for a modern C++ engine. Hazel also uses DirectXCompiler (dxc) — it authors shaders in HLSL, not GLSL. EnTT EnTT Direct corroboration of the ECS choice. Jolt JoltPhysics (3D) + Box2D (2D) Strong corroboration. Also empirically confirms research §7's aside: the 3D lib is Jolt and Box2D is 2D-only — there is no "Box3D." Dear ImGui ImGui (docking branch) + imgui-node-editor Confirms ImGui for editor/debug UI. glm glm Same. shaderc shaderc + shaderc_util Same compiler; Hazel pairs it with SPIRV-Cross (below).

docs.title: Diverges — validated, keeping our choice with reason
docs.text:
• Windowing: Hazel = GLFW; us = SDL3. Research found no verified evidence either way. Keeping SDL3 for its gamepad/audio/haptics/IME breadth (a survival game wants these); Hazel confirms GLFW is a perfectly viable fallback if SDL3 friction appears.
  • Build: Hazel = premake; us = CMake + vcpkg. Keeping CMake+vcpkg for its dependency management and tooling ecosystem; premake is lighter but hands you manual vendored submodules (Hazel vendors ~25 of them).
  • Vulkan SDK: Hazel requires it; us deliberately SDK-free (volk + vcpkg headers + runtime shaderc). Keeping the SDK-free approach — it builds on a clean machine, which Hazel's os.getenv("VULKAN_SDK") does not.
  • Shader language: Hazel = HLSL→dxc; us = GLSL→shaderc. Noted as a real alternative (HLSL+dxc is increasingly the modern default). Not switching now, but reconsider if/when the shader system matures.

docs.title: Worth adopting from Hazel (validated additions, not in the original stack)
docs.text:
• Tracy profiler — adopt early (vcpkg tracy). A frame/zone profiler is high-value infrastructure for a performance-critical voxel engine and cheap to wire in. Best pulled in during §3.
  • SPIRV-Cross — adopt when the shader system needs reflection (auto descriptor-set/pipeline-layout generation). vcpkg spirv-cross.
  • stb (stb_image) — texture/image loading; will be needed for block atlases. vcpkg stb.
  • Deferred / later-phase, noted: MiniAudio (audio), Assimp (non-voxel model import, if ever), yaml-cpp (scene/config serialization — voxel chunks still want binary), msdf-atlas-gen + Freetype (crisp text), magic_enum (reflection-lite utility), NVIDIA Aftermath (GPU crash dumps on the RTX 5090 — proprietary, not in vcpkg).

docs.title: Structural patterns to borrow (Apache-2.0 permits adapting code with attribution)
docs.text: Hazel's module split is a proven shape for exactly this kind of project and matches Dokicraft's intended layout: a core engine library, a separate editor app (ImGui-based), a thin runtime/launcher, and an asset system. Adopt the organization; write our own voxel renderer inside it.

docs.title: Dokicraft Engine Tutorial: A Field Guide For Unreal Developers
docs.text:
This page is meant to teach you how the Dokicraft engine works, from the first line of main() to the pixels in the screenshot below, and how to approach extending it. It's written for an experienced gameplay programmer coming from Unreal Engine. You already know what a frame is, what a PSO is for, and why threading the renderer is hard. What you probably haven't done is own all of it yourself, with no RHI, no RDG, and no engine underneath you. That's the fun part.

Everything in this doc references real code in this repo at time of writing. When the code and this page disagree, trust the code and let us know so we can fix the page.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• How the engine boots, renders, and shuts down, mapped onto the UE concepts you already have.
  • The handful of Vulkan ideas UE's RHI has been hiding from you (and why they're less scary than their reputation).
  • How the voxel scene gets generated and drawn.
  • Concrete recipes for extending the engine: a fly camera, an ImGui HUD, real chunk meshing, textures, physics, and gameplay via ECS.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
Dokicraft is a from-scratch C++20 voxel survival engine targeting Windows and high-end GPUs. Think Minecraft-like gameplay at higher fidelity: smaller voxels, modern lighting, streamed worlds. The architecture decisions came out of a research pass you can read in full, with citations, here:

Research report: research/RESEARCH.md

The current stack, and why:

  • Vulkan 1.3 - The rendering API. We use dynamic rendering and synchronization2, which cut most of the boilerplate Vulkan is infamous for. No render passes, no framebuffer objects.
  • volk - A meta-loader for Vulkan. It loads function pointers at runtime so we don't link against a Vulkan SDK. The SDK isn't required to build or run.
  • VMA (Vulkan Memory Allocator) - AMD's allocator library. It answers "which of the 11 memory types do I allocate this buffer in" so you mostly don't have to care.
  • SDL3 - Windowing and input. Chosen over GLFW for the gamepad, audio, and haptics coverage a survival game will eventually want.
  • shaderc - Runtime GLSL to SPIR-V compilation. Shaders compile when the game boots, which keeps the door open for hot reload.
  • glm - Math. The de facto standard for Vulkan/OpenGL style projects.
  • EnTT - ECS for gameplay code (linked, not yet used in the frame loop).
  • Jolt - Physics (linked, integration comes with the survival gameplay phase).
  • Dear ImGui - Debug and editor UI (in the dependency set, HUD recipe below).

The engine is a static library, doki_engine, consumed by a thin game executable, dokicraft. Here's the module map. GitHub renders this diagram inline; if you're reading locally, any Mermaid viewer works.

flowchart TD
    subgraph game ["dokicraft (game exe)"]
        Main["Main.cpp<br/>owns the loop"]
    end
    subgraph engine ["doki_engine (static lib)"]
        Window["platform/Window<br/>SDL3"]
        Context["render/VulkanContext<br/>instance, device, VMA"]
        Swap["render/Swapchain"]
        Renderer["render/Renderer<br/>frame loop, sync, depth"]
        Pipeline["render/MeshPipeline<br/>+ ShaderCompiler"]
        Mesh["render/GpuMesh<br/>vertex/index buffers"]
        Terrain["scene/Terrain<br/>voxel gen"]
        Camera["scene/Camera"]
    end
    Main --> Window
    Main --> Context
    Main --> Swap
    Main --> Renderer
    Main --> Pipeline
    Main --> Mesh
    Main --> Terrain
    Main --> Camera
    Context --> Swap
    Swap --> Renderer
    Pipeline --> Renderer

Note: the dependency arrows are deliberately shallow. Main.cpp composes everything explicitly, so you can read the whole engine boot top to bottom in one file. There's no reflection, no module registry, and no magic startup order to reverse-engineer.

docs.title: Coming From Unreal: A Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
You don't need a UE-to-Vulkan dictionary memorized, but these mappings will make the rest of the page read faster.

  • FEngineLoop / Tick - Main.cpp owns a plain while (window.pollEvents()) loop. There's no engine loop object. You are the engine loop.
  • UBT + .uproject - CMake presets plus a vcpkg manifest (vcpkg.json). cmake --preset windows-release is roughly "Generate Project Files" and "Build" folded together.
  • RHI - Gone. We call Vulkan directly through volk. The closest thing to an RHI layer is VulkanContext. It's about 300 lines you can read in one sitting.
  • RDG passes and resource transitions - Done by hand with synchronization2 barriers in Renderer::drawFrame. RDG's "declare reads/writes and let the graph schedule" becomes "you write the barrier yourself". It's the single biggest mindset shift. It's also covered in detail below.
  • PSO - VkPipeline, built in MeshPipeline. Same idea, same immutability, same "build at load time, bind at draw time" rhythm. UE's PSO caching pain will feel familiar.
  • Material parameters / uniform buffers - Push constants for now (a tiny, fast constant block baked into the command buffer). Descriptor sets and UBOs arrive when the data outgrows 128 bytes. Both are covered in the recipes.
  • GameThread / RenderThread split - There isn't one yet. One thread does everything. Frames-in-flight (below) is what keeps the GPU busy anyway.
  • FVector and friends - glm. Watch the conventions: this engine is Y-up and right-handed, and one world unit is one voxel. UE is Z-up, left-handed, in centimeters. If you port math from UE muscle memory, swap Y and Z and re-check your cross products.
  • AActor / UActorComponent - Nothing yet. Gameplay will land in EnTT, which is closer to Mass than to Actors. There's a recipe below.
  • Chaos - Jolt, integrated at the survival-gameplay phase. The integration pattern is already researched and documented.
  • Slate / UMG - Dear ImGui for debug UI now, RmlUi (HTML/CSS, fully open source) as the candidate for shipping game UI later.
  • check() / ensure() - VK_CHECK(expr) aborts with the file, line, and failing expression on any Vulkan error. Fail fast and fix fast.

Note: the coordinate and unit differences are the one place UE instincts will actively betray you. When something renders upside down or orbits the wrong way, check the Y-flip in Camera (explained below) before you suspect the matrix math.

docs.title: Step 0: Get It Building
docs.text:
You'll want a working build before reading further so the code excerpts have something to diff against.

  1. Prerequisites: Visual Studio 2022 or newer with the C++ workload, CMake 3.28+, Ninja, and Git. No Vulkan SDK needed, just a Vulkan-capable GPU driver.
  2. Clone and bootstrap:
git clone https://github.com/defessler/Dokicraft.git
cd Dokicraft
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg.git extern/vcpkg
extern\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat -disableMetrics
  1. Build and run. From any shell:
pwsh -File Tools/Build.ps1 -Preset windows-release
build\windows-release\bin\dokicraft.exe

Tools/Build.ps1 finds Visual Studio with vswhere and enters the VS dev shell for you, which is what makes Ninja plus cl work outside a Developer Command Prompt. The first configure builds all 16 dependencies from source through vcpkg and takes a few minutes. After that, builds are incremental and fast.

A few build-system details worth knowing because they'll bite you if you fight them:

  • vcpkg manifest mode - vcpkg.json at the repo root declares dependencies with a pinned baseline, so a clean clone always resolves the same versions. Think of it as the dependency half of a .uproject.
  • Warnings as errors, scoped - Project targets compile with /W4 /WX, but vcpkg headers are included via MSVC's /external:anglebrackets /external:W0, so third-party warnings can't break our build. Include project headers with quotes and dependencies with angle brackets to keep that split working.
  • VK_NO_PROTOTYPES - Defined project-wide. It tells the Vulkan headers not to declare linkable function prototypes, because volk supplies every entry point at runtime. If you ever see "unresolved external symbol vkCreateDevice", something bypassed volk.

docs.title: The Six Building Blocks
docs.text: To understand the engine, you need to understand six main building blocks. Each one is a class you can read in full in a few minutes. Each maps to something you already know from UE.

docs.title: 1. Window (SDL3)
docs.text:
This is where the OS window and the event pump live. It's the analog of the game viewport plus the platform application layer, minus about two hundred thousand lines.

You can find the implementation here: src/engine/src/platform/Window.cpp

The interesting part is how little there is. pollEvents drains SDL's queue and returns false when it's time to quit:

bool Window::pollEvents()
{
    SDL_Event event;
    while (SDL_PollEvent(&event))
    {
        if (event.type == SDL_EVENT_QUIT)
        {
            return false;
        }
        ...
        if (event.type == SDL_EVENT_KEY_DOWN && event.key.key == SDLK_ESCAPE)
        {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

In UE terms, this loop is where the platform message pump, the input subsystem, and RequestEngineExit all collapse into one function. When you add real input handling (see the fly camera recipe), this is the function that grows.

docs.title: 2. VulkanContext (Instance, Device, Queue, VMA)
docs.text:
This owns everything that lives for the whole session: the VkInstance, the physical and logical device, the graphics queue, and the VMA allocator. It's the closest thing we have to an RHI. It's created once in main() and torn down at exit.

You can find the implementation here: src/engine/src/render/VulkanContext.cpp

Three things in it deserve your attention.

First, the volk boot dance. Vulkan has no import library in our build, so entry points load in three waves: volkInitialize() finds the loader DLL, volkLoadInstance() loads instance-level functions after the instance exists, and volkLoadDevice() loads device-level functions after the device exists. The constructor reads exactly in that order:

VK_CHECK(volkInitialize());
createInstance();
volkLoadInstance(m_instance);
createSurface(window);
pickPhysicalDevice();
createLogicalDevice();
volkLoadDevice(m_device);

Second, device selection. This machine exposes three adapters (an RTX 5090, an Intel iGPU, and a Parsec virtual display), and naive "take device zero" code will happily render your voxels on the wrong one. pickPhysicalDevice requires a graphics-and-present queue, the swapchain extension, and the Vulkan 1.3 features we depend on, then scores discrete GPUs a thousand points ahead of everything else. The log tells you what won:

[doki][INFO ] Selected GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (Vulkan 1.4.341)

Third, the feature request. We turn on dynamicRendering and synchronization2 (Vulkan 1.3 core), plus bufferDeviceAddress and descriptorIndexing from 1.2, which the GPU-driven rendering phase will want. Requesting features at device creation is Vulkan's version of checking GRHISupportsX flags, except you ask up front. The device simply refuses to be created if the hardware can't do it.

Note: validation layers (Vulkan's equivalent of the D3D debug layer plus a very good RHI validation suite) only exist if a Vulkan SDK is installed. The engine detects their absence and runs without them rather than failing. If you install the LunarG SDK, they light up automatically on the next run. Treat any validation error as a real bug.

docs.title: 3. Swapchain
docs.text:
The swapchain is the backbuffer chain: the set of images the OS compositor will actually put on screen. UE hides this behind the viewport; here it's about 150 lines.

You can find the implementation here: src/engine/src/render/Swapchain.cpp

Decisions it makes, and why:

  • Format - Prefers VK_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_SRGB, so the hardware handles gamma on write and our fragment shaders think in linear color. Same convention UE renders with.
  • Present mode - Prefers mailbox (low-latency triple buffering, no tearing) and falls back to FIFO, which is plain vsync and the only mode Vulkan guarantees everywhere.
  • Image count - Asks for minimum plus one to reduce acquire stalls.

There are no framebuffer or render pass objects anywhere in it. Dynamic rendering means we attach image views directly at draw time, which removes the most confusing third of classic Vulkan tutorials.

docs.title: 4. Renderer (The Frame Loop)
docs.text:
This is the heart of the engine and the file to read most carefully. It owns per-frame command buffers, the synchronization objects, and a depth buffer. Every frame it runs acquire, record, submit, and present.

You can find the implementation here: src/engine/src/render/Renderer.cpp

It deliberately doesn't know what a voxel is. The scene hands it a callback:

using RecordSceneFn = std::function<void(VkCommandBuffer cmd, VkExtent2D extent)>;
void drawFrame(const float clearColor[4], const RecordSceneFn& recordScene);

The renderer opens the "render pass" (clears color and depth, sets up attachments), calls your callback to record draws, closes it, and handles presentation. It's a tiny, explicit version of what RDG's pass lambdas do. A full frame walkthrough gets its own section below.

docs.title: 5. MeshPipeline And ShaderCompiler
docs.text:
MeshPipeline builds the one graphics pipeline the scene currently needs: vertex color times a directional light, depth tested, no culling yet. ShaderCompiler wraps shaderc so the GLSL compiles when the pipeline is constructed.

You can find the implementations here: src/engine/src/render/MeshPipeline.cpp src/engine/src/render/ShaderCompiler.cpp

The shaders are embedded GLSL string literals in MeshPipeline.cpp at time of writing. That's a deliberate stage-one choice: no asset paths to break while the pipeline count is one. They'll move to shaders/ files once hot reload lands. The fragment shader is a plain diffuse with an ambient floor:

vec3 normal = normalize(vNormal);
vec3 toLight = normalize(-pc.lightDirection.xyz);
float diffuse = max(dot(normal, toLight), 0.0);
float ambient = 0.28;
float intensity = ambient + (1.0 - ambient) * diffuse;
outColor = vec4(vColor * intensity, 1.0);

Camera and light data travel as push constants, which is Vulkan's fast path for small per-draw data:

struct MeshPushConstants
{
    glm::mat4 viewProj;       // 64 bytes
    glm::vec4 lightDirection; // 16 bytes
};

That's 80 bytes against Vulkan's guaranteed minimum budget of 128. We're comfortably inside the portable limit. When per-draw data outgrows it (and it will, the moment textures arrive), the uniform buffer recipe below is the graduation path.

One UE-relevant note on pipeline state: everything except viewport and scissor is baked into the VkPipeline at creation. Blend mode, depth test, vertex layout, and shaders are immutable per pipeline, exactly like a PSO. Viewport and scissor are declared dynamic so window resizes don't force a pipeline rebuild.

docs.title: 6. GpuMesh, Terrain, And Camera
docs.text:
GpuMesh uploads vertex and index data into VMA-allocated buffers and issues the indexed draw. The upload currently writes straight into host-visible mapped memory:

VmaAllocationCreateInfo allocInfo{};
allocInfo.usage = VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO;
allocInfo.flags = VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_SEQUENTIAL_WRITE_BIT |
                  VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_MAPPED_BIT;

On a modern card with resizable BAR this lands in memory that's both host-visible and device-local. That's fast enough for static scene geometry. Staged uploads through a transfer queue come when chunk streaming does, so treat the current path as "good enough on purpose".

Terrain generates the placeholder world: a 32x32 grid of columns, heights from deterministic value noise blended with a couple of sine waves, one colored cube per solid voxel, banded grass, dirt, and stone by depth. The same seed always produces the same terrain, which is what makes the smoke test's screenshot comparisons meaningful.

You can find the generator here: src/engine/src/scene/Terrain.cpp

Camera is a look-at perspective camera with the two lines that trip up everyone who comes to Vulkan from anywhere else:

glm::mat4 proj = glm::perspective(fovYRadians, aspect, nearZ, farZ);
proj[1][1] *= -1.0F;    // Vulkan clip-space Y points down

We also define GLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE project-wide because Vulkan's depth range is 0 to 1, not OpenGL's -1 to 1. If you remove either of these you'll get an upside-down scene or a broken depth test. Now you know which file to check first.

docs.title: A Frame, From Acquire To Present
docs.text:
This is the part UE never let you touch. Here's the sequence Renderer::drawFrame runs, then the three ideas inside it that matter.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CPU as CPU (drawFrame)
    participant GPU as GPU queue
    participant WSI as Swapchain/Present
    CPU->>CPU: wait fence (frame N-2 done)
    CPU->>WSI: vkAcquireNextImageKHR
    WSI-->>CPU: image index + imageAvailable semaphore
    CPU->>CPU: record commands<br/>(barrier, clear, draws, barrier)
    CPU->>GPU: vkQueueSubmit2<br/>wait imageAvailable, signal renderFinished, signal fence
    GPU->>GPU: execute command buffer
    CPU->>WSI: vkQueuePresentKHR (waits renderFinished)
    WSI-->>WSI: image on screen

First idea: frames in flight. The CPU doesn't wait for the GPU to finish a frame before starting the next one. We keep two frames of command buffers and sync objects (kFramesInFlight = 2). The CPU records frame N+1 while the GPU draws frame N. The fence at the top of drawFrame is the throttle: it blocks only if the GPU is a full two frames behind. This is the same pipelining UE gets from its render thread, achieved with zero extra threads.

Second idea: semaphores vs fences. Both are new if the RHI always did it for you. A fence lets the GPU signal the CPU ("that command buffer is done, you can reuse it"). A semaphore lets one GPU operation wait on another without the CPU involved ("don't start rendering until the swapchain image is actually available, don't present until rendering is done"). One detail worth copying if you ever write this yourself: the render-finished semaphores are per swapchain image, not per frame in flight, which avoids a subtle validation error when the two counts differ.

Third idea: image layout transitions. Vulkan images live in explicit layouts (undefined, color attachment, present source, etc.). You insert barriers to move between them. This is what RDG transitions compile down to. Our frame does three: acquired image to color attachment, depth image to depth attachment, and rendered image to present source. The helper in Renderer.cpp shows the synchronization2 shape:

transitionImage(cmd, swapImage,
    VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_UNDEFINED, VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OPTIMAL,
    VK_IMAGE_ASPECT_COLOR_BIT,
    VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_TOP_OF_PIPE_BIT, 0,
    VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OUTPUT_BIT,
    VK_ACCESS_2_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_WRITE_BIT);

Read it as "everything before this point in stage X with access Y must complete before anything after it in stage Z with access W, and change the layout while you're at it". Once that sentence parses, you can read any barrier in any Vulkan codebase.

Resize is handled where acquire or present return VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DATE_KHR: rebuild the swapchain, the per-image semaphores, and the depth buffer, then skip the frame. Minimized windows just skip drawing entirely (see the loop in Main.cpp).

docs.title: How The Scene Gets Assembled
docs.text:
Main.cpp is short enough to read whole. Here's just the shape:

doki::Window window("Dokicraft", 1280, 720);
doki::VulkanContext context(window.handle());
doki::Swapchain swapchain(context, width, height);
doki::Renderer renderer(context, swapchain, window);
doki::MeshPipeline pipeline(context, renderer.colorFormat(), renderer.depthFormat());

const doki::TerrainMesh terrain = doki::generateTerrain(32, 1337U);
const doki::GpuMesh mesh(context.allocator(), terrain.vertices, terrain.indices);

while (window.pollEvents())
{
    // orbit camera, build push constants...
    renderer.drawFrame(skyBlue, [&](VkCommandBuffer cmd, VkExtent2D extent) {
        // set viewport + scissor
        pipeline.bind(cmd);
        pipeline.pushConstants(cmd, push);
        mesh.draw(cmd);
    });
}

Construction order is destruction order reversed. Every object takes what it needs by reference. If you've fought UE subsystem initialization order, you'll appreciate how boring this is. The camera orbits the terrain on a timer for now so the scene reads as 3D before any input handling exists. Making it player-controlled is the first recipe below.

docs.title: Extending It: Recipes
docs.text: Each recipe says why you'd do it and where it hooks in, then sketches the code. The sketches are written for this codebase but they're not in the repo yet. Treat them as a starting point and feel free to reshape them.

docs.title: Recipe: A Fly Camera
docs.text:
It's the natural first project. It touches input, per-frame state, and math all at once. Grow Window to expose input state instead of just a quit flag:

struct InputState
{
    glm::vec2 mouseDelta{0.0F};
    bool keyDown[SDL_SCANCODE_COUNT] = {};
    bool quit = false;
};

Fill it in pollEvents from SDL_EVENT_MOUSE_MOTION (accumulate event.motion.xrel and yrel) and SDL_EVENT_KEY_DOWN / SDL_EVENT_KEY_UP. Call SDL_SetWindowRelativeMouseMode(m_window, true) for FPS-style mouse capture. Then keep yaw and pitch in Main.cpp and rebuild the camera each frame:

yaw += input.mouseDelta.x * kSensitivity;
pitch = glm::clamp(pitch - input.mouseDelta.y * kSensitivity, -1.5F, 1.5F);

const glm::vec3 forward{std::cos(pitch) * std::cos(yaw), std::sin(pitch),
                        std::cos(pitch) * std::sin(yaw)};
const glm::vec3 right = glm::normalize(glm::cross(forward, {0.0F, 1.0F, 0.0F}));

if (input.keyDown[SDL_SCANCODE_W]) { position += forward * speed * dt; }
// ... A/S/D/Q/E ...
camera.position = position;
camera.target = position + forward;

Remember the handedness note from the Rosetta Stone: Y is up here and the cross product order above matters.

docs.title: Recipe: The ImGui Debug HUD
docs.text:
The imgui vcpkg dependency is already in the manifest with the sdl3-binding and vulkan-binding features, so the backends are compiled and waiting. Wire-up steps: initialize ImGui_ImplSDL3_InitForVulkan and ImGui_ImplVulkan_Init after the renderer exists, feed SDL events to ImGui_ImplSDL3_ProcessEvent inside Window::pollEvents, and record ImGui_ImplVulkan_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData(), cmd) at the end of the scene callback so the HUD draws over the world.

IMPORTANT: the vcpkg ImGui Vulkan backend is compiled without VK_NO_PROTOTYPES, while our engine loads everything through volk. Call ImGui_ImplVulkan_LoadFunctions before ImGui_ImplVulkan_Init and forward it to volk, or every ImGui Vulkan call will crash at startup:

ImGui_ImplVulkan_LoadFunctions(VK_API_VERSION_1_3,
    [](const char* name, void* userData) {
        return vkGetInstanceProcAddr(static_cast<VkInstance>(userData), name);
    },
    context.instance());

ImGui's Vulkan backend also wants a descriptor pool and your attachment formats (use renderer.colorFormat() and renderer.depthFormat() with its dynamic rendering path). The official example in the ImGui repo, examples/example_sdl3_vulkan, is the reference to crib from.

docs.title: Recipe: Real Chunks And Binary Greedy Meshing
docs.text:
This is the milestone that turns "a scene" into "a world". It's where the research earns its keep. The current Terrain emits six faces per solid voxel with no culling, which is fine for 32x32 and hopeless at scale. The plan:

  1. Store voxels in fixed-size chunks. The research favors small render chunks (Project Ascendant uses 8x8x8) grouped into larger streaming regions, but a straightforward first cut is a 62x62x62 payload in a 64x64x64 array, because the meshing algorithm wants a one-voxel neighbor apron.
  2. Replace cube emission with face culling: only emit a face where solid meets air. That alone cuts geometry by an order of magnitude.
  3. Then adopt binary greedy meshing. Pack solidity into 64-bit column masks so face culling becomes bit math (faces = column & ~(column >> 1) and friends), then merge adjacent same-type faces into large quads with more bit scans. The reference implementation meshes a whole chunk in 50 to 200 microseconds single-threaded and outputs 8-byte packed quads. The algorithm is readable in an afternoon, check it out: https://github.com/cgerikj/binary-greedy-meshing
  4. Emit packed quads instead of fat vertices. Six bits each for x, y, z, width, and height, plus a face id and a voxel type. Unpack in the vertex shader by indexing with gl_VertexIndex. Your Vertex struct shrinks from 36 bytes per vertex to 8 bytes per quad.
  5. One draw call per chunk is fine for dozens of chunks. The endgame per the research is one vkCmdDrawIndexedIndirectCount for everything, with a compute shader writing the draw list (GPU-driven culling). bufferDeviceAddress and descriptorIndexing are already enabled on the device for exactly this.

Note: keep the deterministic seed discipline from generateTerrain when you build real worldgen. The smoke test anchors on a fixed-seed world. Future you will want screenshots that diff cleanly.

docs.title: Recipe: Textures (Your First Descriptor Set)
docs.text:
Push constants can't hold a texture. This recipe forces the remaining big Vulkan concept: descriptors. The five-step shape, using stb from the research stack (add the stb port to vcpkg.json):

  1. Load pixels with stbi_load.
  2. Create a VkImage through VMA, copy pixels in, and transition it to VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_SHADER_READ_ONLY_OPTIMAL with a one-shot command buffer.
  3. Create a VkImageView and a VkSampler (nearest-neighbor filtering is the correct look for a voxel atlas).
  4. Create a VkDescriptorSetLayout with one combined image sampler binding, a VkDescriptorPool, allocate a set, and point it at your view and sampler with vkUpdateDescriptorSets.
  5. Add the layout to the VkPipelineLayout in MeshPipeline, bind the set with vkCmdBindDescriptorSets before drawing, and sample it in the fragment shader via a layout(set = 0, binding = 0) uniform sampler2D.

A descriptor set is just a bundle of shader-visible resource handles. If you think of it as "the Vulkan spelling of a material's texture parameters", you have the right intuition. UV coordinates ride in as a new Vertex attribute (or come along for free once you're unpacking greedy-meshed quads in the vertex shader).

docs.title: Recipe: From Push Constants To Uniform Buffers
docs.text: When per-frame data outgrows 128 bytes (camera plus fog plus lighting rig plus time), move it into a UBO: one VkBuffer per frame in flight (host-visible, persistently mapped, just like GpuMesh does), written by the CPU each frame, exposed to shaders through the same descriptor machinery as the texture recipe. Per-frame duplication exists for the same reason kFramesInFlight does: frame N+1's CPU writes must not stomp a buffer the GPU is still reading for frame N.

docs.title: Recipe: Physics With Jolt
docs.text:
Jolt is already linked. The integration pattern for voxel terrain comes from Jolt's own author (the research report links the full discussion):

  • One Body with a StaticCompoundShape per chunk.
  • A small set of shared BoxShape instances reused across every block of the same size, not one shape allocation per block.
  • Batch-add bodies and call PhysicsSystem::OptimizeBroadPhase after loading a wave of chunks.
  • Rebuild a chunk's compound shape when it's edited, and wake sleeping bodies nearby.

He confirms 100k static bodies is comfortable territory. A body per chunk scales well past anything we'll need for a while. Step the simulation once per frame from the main loop (PhysicsSystem::Update with fixed 1/60 collision steps). Then read body transforms when you build render matrices. Character movement wants Jolt's CharacterVirtual, which is the rough equivalent of UE's CharacterMovementComponent mode of interacting with the world, minus the networking.

docs.title: Recipe: Gameplay In EnTT
docs.text:
EnTT is closer to Mass than to Actors: entities are integer ids, components are plain structs, and systems are free functions iterating views. The pattern we suggest for this codebase:

struct Transform { glm::vec3 position; glm::quat rotation; };
struct Velocity { glm::vec3 linear; };

void integrateMovement(entt::registry& world, float dt)
{
    for (auto [entity, transform, velocity] : world.view<Transform, Velocity>().each())
    {
        transform.position += velocity.linear * dt;
    }
}

Call systems explicitly from the main loop in a fixed order. Resist the urge to build a scheduler until you have enough systems to need one. The mental shift from UE is that nothing Ticks itself: there's no PrimaryActorTick, just functions you call, which makes execution order a thing you read instead of a thing you debug.

docs.title: Recipe: Tracy Profiling
docs.text: Once frame times matter (the meshing milestone), add the tracy vcpkg port, wrap the main loop phases in ZoneScoped markers, and run the Tracy server app to get UE Insights-quality flame graphs with about ten lines of integration. The research flagged this as worth adopting early. We agree.

docs.title: Conventions And Gotchas
docs.text:
House rules so your extensions land cleanly. The full profile lives in CLAUDE.md.

  • Style - 4-space indent, 120-column lines, Allman braces, always brace single statements. .clang-format at the repo root enforces the mechanical parts. Run it on anything you touch.
  • Naming - PascalCase types and functions, camelCase locals and parameters, m_ members, SCREAMING_CASE constants, everything under namespace doki.
  • Copyright - Every source file starts with // Copyright (c) defessler.
  • Include order trap - volk before VMA, always. vk_mem_alloc.h binds to whatever Vulkan declarations it sees. It must see volk's. The headers that need both already do it correctly, so follow their lead.
  • glm defines - GLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE and GLM_FORCE_RADIANS are set on the engine target. Don't include glm in a way that dodges them.
  • The multi-GPU trap - Never index physical devices directly. pickPhysicalDevice exists because this dev machine will hand you a virtual display adapter if you let it.
  • No per-frame allocations - The frame loop allocates nothing after startup. It should stay that way as far as practical. It's much easier to keep a loop allocation-free than to win the memory back later.

docs.title: Where This Is Headed
docs.text:
The roadmap, decisions, and their rationale live in two documents that are kept current as the engine grows:

Plan and ledger: Docs/PLAN.md

Research report with citations: research/RESEARCH.md

The near-term arc: real chunked worldgen with binary greedy meshing, GPU compute culling with indirect draws, then the lighting jump (sun plus ambient occlusion first, probe-based DDGI later). The far-field plan is non-polygonal (per-voxel raycast quads, per the Ascendant writeup). Hardware ray tracing on RTX-class cards is an open question the research left explicitly unresolved. Plenty of room to leave your mark.
